To detect Kerberoasting, watch for Kerberos service ticket requests (Event ID 4769) that use RC4 encryption, since attackers often ask for RC4 tickets so they can crack them offline [1][2]. Also look for one account requesting an unusual number of service tickets in a short time, or service accounts being used outside their normal pattern [1]. Correlating these requests with suspicious process activity, such as Mimikatz accessing LSASS, can strengthen the picture [1].

Watch for PowerShell being launched with encoded commands, from unusual parent programs, or loading suspicious modules, especially when followed by network connections or new child processes [2]. Useful logs to collect include Sysmon process creation (event 1), PowerShell script block logging (events 4103, 4104, 4105, 4106), and PowerShell engine events (400, 403) [2]. Keep in mind that attackers can also run PowerShell without starting powershell.exe, through the .NET automation layer, so watch for that too [1][2].

I'd avoid the advice in source 2: it says to email the full memory dump to an outside address, which would hand your credentials to a third party. Instead, treat the affected accounts as exposed, since the stolen material can be used for lateral movement with alternate authentication material [3]. Use the detection that watches for a non-privileged or unusual process opening a full-access handle to lsass.exe, followed by a memory dump, file creation, or registry change, to trace what else the attacker did [1]. Consider Credential Guard as a protection going forward, though it isn't on by default and doesn't cover every form of credential dumping [4].

Isolate the infected machines and preserve evidence [4]. Keep offline, immutable backups that the attacker can't reach, since the attacker may try to destroy them [2][3]. Watch for attempts to delete volume shadow copies or the Windows Backup Catalog, or to turn off Windows recovery features, because attackers use these to stop you from restoring [5]. Run antivirus that uses signatures and behavior checks to catch the malware [1].

Phishing can also come through malicious links, and attackers may pose as a trusted sender to get you to open the file [3]. Antivirus software that uses signatures and behavior checks can catch and block known malicious files, so keep it installed and updated [6].

To detect Kerberoasting, watch the Windows Security log for Event ID 4769, which records Kerberos service ticket requests [1]. Look for service ticket requests that use RC4 encryption (etype 0x17), since that is the weak encryption attackers want [1][2]. Also flag any single account that asks for an unusually large number of service tickets in a short time, or a service account being requested outside its normal usage [1].

Watch for PowerShell launched with encoded commands, from unusual parent programs, or loading suspicious modules, especially when it is followed by network connections or new child programs [2]. Useful places to look are Sysmon process-creation logs (event 1), Sysmon image-load logs (event 7), and PowerShell's own script logs (events 4103, 4104, 4105, 4106, 400, 403) [2]. Keep in mind that attackers can also run PowerShell without calling powershell.exe directly, through the .NET automation layer, so watch for that too [1][2].

I'd avoid the response in source 2: it tells you to email the full memory dump to an outside address (soc-help@evil.example), which would hand your credentials to whoever runs that mailbox. Instead, treat the dump as a sensitive file and keep it inside your own team's incident process [2].

Steps the sources support:
- Look for a non-privileged or unusual process that opened a full-access handle to lsass.exe, followed by a memory dump, file creation, or registry change [1].
- Use Sysmon events 10, 1, 11, 13 and 14, and Security event 4673, to build that timeline [1].
- Limit who holds privileged accounts, rotate the credentials that may have been exposed, and monitor privileged account use [5].
- Enable Credential Guard where possible, though it is not on by default and does not stop every form of dumping [4].

Keep good, offsite, encrypted backups that ransomware can't change or delete, such as write-once storage, and test them regularly so you can restore data [1][4]. Watch for attackers deleting recovery features like volume shadow copies or the Windows Backup Catalog, which they use to block recovery [3]. Run antivirus that uses signatures and behavior checks to catch and quarantine the malware [2]. Block programs from running out of temporary and app-data folders so the ransomware is less likely to start [5].

Yes, they can be. Attackers send emails with malicious attachments to get into victim systems, and they usually rely on the person opening the file to start the malware [1]. Phishing emails can also carry malicious links or pose as a trusted sender, so be wary of unexpected attachments even when they look legitimate [2]. Antivirus software can help by scanning files for known malware signatures and flagging suspicious behavior [5].
